title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 10: How GMA Can Prolong Her Stay
keywords: How GMA Can Prolong Her Stay
primary_topics: Chapter 10 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1) -- CJP's January 31, 2010 Inquirer column warning that a partial 'failure of proclamation' from automated-election glitches could open a path for GMA to remain in power past June 30, 2010

sub_topics: The occasion: the CBCP, through its new president Bishop Nereo Odchimar, urged the Comelec to prepare 'fallback positions' for automated-election glitches -- which CJP takes as a 'reverberation' of his own call to 'prepare for manual polls now'

PCOS tests inadequate: though Comelec Chair Melo was 'still open' to reverting to manual polls and Commissioner Larrazabal said the Precinct Count Optical Scan machines passed lab and field tests, those tests 'involved only very few PCOS' unrepresentative of the total '82,200 machines'

Why credible testing was impossible: proper tests require machines 'precinct specific' -- calibrated to count the actual ballots (with local candidates' names) for each of the country's 1,630 towns, correctly printed, delivered, inserted and calibrated -- and 'Comelec has no more time for these crucial tests,' making 'hybrids' risky too

The 'no proc' mechanism: Comelec admitted possible automation problems in 'about 30 percent of the country,' and problems in several towns and cities 'when put together' could legally trigger a 'failure of proclamation' for president, vice-president and senators

The arithmetic: in a tight race (Villar closing on Aquino), assuming a winning margin no greater than 10 percent of the roughly 40 million votes cast (a four-million 'landslide'), glitches in 15 percent of the country would leave six million votes uncounted -- enough to 'overhaul the lead,' so 'no one would be proclaimed winner' for national offices

How GMA stays: with no problems in the other 85 percent, local winners -- governors, mayors, congressmen, 'including putative Rep. Gloria M. Arroyo' -- would be proclaimed, the House could convene and elect a speaker, and with the presidency, vice-presidency, Senate presidency and speakership all expiring June 30, 2010, GMA could claim to be 'holdover' president and, once elected speaker, continue as 'acting' president per the constitutional succession
Why the Senate could not fill the gap: the 12 holdover senators (terms ending 2013) would 'not constitute a quorum,' and the new senators would suffer the same 'no-proc' fate

The endgame and the close: a failed election in 15 percent of the country could make GMA holdover then acting president, dovetailing with a Cha-cha (without a functioning Senate) installing a parliamentary government that elects her prime minister -- all destined for the Supreme Court, which explains the 'political maneuverings' over the selection of the new chief justice; the alternatives (martial law, military takeover, people power, civil strife) prompt his closing prayer, 'Heaven help our country'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1), CJP's January 31, 2010 Inquirer column, warns that a partial 'failure of proclamation' from automated-election glitches could open a path for GMA to stay in power past June 30, 2010. Echoing the CBCP's plea (via new president Bishop Odchimar) for Comelec 'fallback positions,' he urges the commission to 'prepare for manual polls now,' arguing it can 'no longer perfect its automation system in time' for the May 10 polls: the PCOS machines were tested only in small, unrepresentative numbers -- not the 82,200 to be deployed -- and never made 'precinct specific,' calibrated to the actual ballots for each of the 1,630 towns, for which 'Comelec has no more time.' He then builds the 'no proc' scenario: the Comelec admitted possible problems in 'about 30 percent of the country,' and even a 15-percent failure would leave roughly six million votes uncounted -- in a tight race (Villar closing on Aquino) with a winning margin under four million, those votes would be 'determinative,' so no one could be proclaimed president, vice-president or senator. Meanwhile, with the other 85 percent unaffected, local winners -- including 'putative Rep. Gloria M. Arroyo' -- would be proclaimed, and the House could elect a speaker; with the presidency, vice-presidency, Senate presidency and speakership all expiring June 30, 2010, GMA could claim to be 'holdover' president and, once elected speaker, continue as 'acting' president under the constitutional succession, the depleted Senate lacking a quorum to intervene. Such a vacancy, he warns, could dovetail with a Senate-less parliamentary Cha-cha that makes her prime minister -- all destined for the Supreme Court, which is why 'political maneuverings abound' over the selection of the new chief justice. Confronting the alternatives -- martial law, military takeover, people power, civil strife -- he ends not with a forecast but with a prayer: 'Heaven help our country.'
